## Results

### An in vitro model of deep-layer glutamatergic neurons

To investigate the molecular mechanisms involved in the onset and progression of TDP-43 proteinopathy, we developed an in vitro model of highly homogeneous murine upper motor neurons (UMNs), i.e., glutamatergic neurons of layers V and VI, amenable to lentiviral transduction with human TDP-43, wild-type (wt) or carrying an ALS-mutation (Gitcho et al., 2008). To obtain primary cortical cultures enriched in glutamatergic neurons of layers V and VI, cells were isolated from the cerebral cortex of mouse embryos harvested at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5), a developmental stage characterized in vivo by a low number of GABAergic neurons and glial cells in the prospective cerebral cortex. Indeed, the immunostaining performed at 3 DIV (Supplementary Figure 1A) revealed that virtually all cells were positive for the neuron-specific β3-tubulin (Ab: TuJ1), and 97% of them stained double-positive for the T-Box Brain Transcription Factor 1 (TBR1), an early marker of deep-layer glutamatergic neurons (Bedogni et al., 2010).

## Significance Statement

Altered RNA metabolism induced by transactivating response element DNA-binding protein of 43 kDa (TDP-43) loss-of-function (LOF) has been suggested to be a core disease mechanism in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Pathogenic mutations in TARDBP cause ALS and FTLD; thus, these mutations are considered to induce TDP-43 LOF. Here, using a human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based model, we found that the pathogenic K263E mutation disrupted RNA processing events in neurons, reflecting TDP-43 LOF. Interestingly, in contrast to neuronal cultures, mutated TDP-43 remained functional in nonneuronal cells, including iPSCs and neural progenitors. This finding indicates an unprecedented neuron-specific LOF of TDP-43 that potentially accounts for the CNS-selective lesions in patients with ALS/FTLD.

## Introduction

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, leading to a progressive loss of motor function.

These processes allow precise spatial and temporal control of translation and are mediated by RNA binding proteins (RBPs), including those known to be associated with neurodegenerative diseases. L224: ## Abstract
L225: Neurons rely on messenger RNA (mRNA) transport and local translation to facilitate rapid protein synthesis in processes far from the cell body. These processes allow precise spatial and temporal control of translation and are mediated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), including those associated with neurodegenerative diseases.
L226: Here, we use proteomics, transcriptomics, and microscopy to investigate the impact of RBP depletion on mRNA transport and local translation in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons. We find thousands of transcripts enriched in neurites and that many of these transcripts are locally translated, possibly due to the shorter length of transcripts in neurites.
L227: Loss of frontotemporal dementia/amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (FTD/ALS)-associated RBPs TDP-43 and hnRNPA1 induce distinct alterations in the neuritic proteome and transcriptome. TDP-43 knockdown (KD) leads to slightly increased neuritic mRNA and translation, while hnRNPA1 loss has more moderate effects on local mRNA profiles, possibly due to compensation by hnRNPA3.
L228: These results highlight the crucial role of FTD/ALS-associated RBPs in mRNA transport and local translation in neurons and the importance of these processes in neuron health and disease.

L234: ## Introduction
L235: Due to their long axons and need to quickly respond to stimuli, neurons transport messenger RNAs (mRNAs) to axons and dendrites to rapidly and efficiently synthesize new proteins at distal sites. This strict spatial and temporal control of translation is regulated in part by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) [【33†1】]. RBPs bind to mRNAs early in their life cycle and participate in splicing, stabilization, transport, and translation of those transcripts [【34†2】, 【35†3】].
L236: Through recognition of binding motifs and formation of mRNA transport granules, RBPs shuttle mRNA to distal processes where the transcripts undergo local translation to synthesize proteins [【36†4】]. Characterization of the transcripts transported and locally translated in neurites is gaining interest and studies have examined localization and translation of individual transcripts [【37†5–9】]. Others have taken unbiased omics approaches [【38†10–13】].
L237: These studies often find cytoskeletal, ribosomal, neuron function, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial, and neuronal growth protein transcripts are neurite localized or are actively translated in axons and dendrites. Further, the neurite transcriptome is highly correlated with the neurite proteome, and transcripts found in neurites are often also locally translated [【38†10】, 【39†14】].
L238: While these studies represent large steps forward in our understanding of mRNA transport and local translation in neurons, the majority have been performed in rodent neurons [【37†5–12】, 【39†14–20】]. To our knowledge, although unbiased, whole transcriptome identification of transported mRNAs has only been performed in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons a few times [【40†16】, 【41†21】], this has not been paired with the identification of locally translated proteins.
L239: In addition to their role in mRNA transport and local translation, RBPs are associated with neurodegeneration. Mutations in RBPs, although rare, are causative of frontotemporal dementia/amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (FTD/ALS) [【42†22】]. Even in cases without a clear genetic cause, ∼40%–50% of FTD cases and >97% of ALS cases have inclusions of one RBP, TDP-43 [【43†23】]. These inclusions can sequester other RBPs, potentially leading to decreased RBP levels [【44†24】].
L240: Further, although some FTD/ALS-associated RBP mutations alter mRNA transport of specific transcripts [【45†25–27】], the role of loss-of-function of FTD/ALS-associated RBPs on mRNA transport and local translation has not been systematically evaluated. FTD/ALS mutations in RBPs have both gain and loss-of-function mechanisms [【42†22】], making it difficult to decipher whether phenotypic changes associated with disease mutations are associated with loss- or gain-of-function mechanisms.
L241: As such, we decided to focus on examining the effect of loss of FTD/ALS-associated RBPs TDP-43 and hnRNPA1 on mRNA transport and local translation.
L242: Here, we characterize the neuritic proteome, transcriptome, and translatome in human iPSC-derived cortical-like neurons (i^{3}Neurons) [【46†28】]. We find thousands of transcripts are transported and locally translated in i^{3}Neurons. We then use CRISPRi to model loss-of-function of the RBPs TDP-43 and hnRNPA1. Through proteomics, transcriptomics, and microscopy we obtain a comprehensive picture of the effect of loss of TDP-43 and hnRNPA1 on mRNA transport and local translation in i^{3}Neurons.
L243: ## Materials and methods
L244: ### iPSC maintenance and differentiation
L245: All policies of the NIH Intramural research program were followed for the procurement and use of human iPS cells. iPSCs were previously engineered to express mouse neurogenin 2 (NGN2) under a doxycycline-inducible promoter [【46†28】]. iPSCs were maintained and differentiated as previously described [【47†29】]. Briefly, iPSCs were maintained on human embryonic stem cell-qualified Matrigel (Corning, 354277) coated plates in Essential 8 (E8, Gibco, A1517001) in a 37°C incubator with 5% CO_{2}.
L246: Media was replaced every 1–2 days. Cells were passaged with 5–10 min accutase (Gibco, A1110501) treatment at 37°C. Accutase was removed and cells were plated in E8 supplemented with 50 nM Chroman 1 (MedChemExpress, HY-15392) to promote survival of single cells. Chroman 1 was removed when cells grew into colonies of 5–10 cells.
L247: For neuronal differentiation, cells were digested in Accutase at 37°C for 5–10 min and resuspended in neuronal induction media [Knockout Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) F12 (Gibco, 12660012), 1× N2 supplement (Gibco, 17502048), 1× nonessential amino acids (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11140 050), 1× Glutamax (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 35050-061), 2 μg/ml doxycycline (Sigma–Aldrich, D9891), 50 nM Chroman 1]. On days 1 and 2, fresh induction media was added to cells.
L248: Day 3, cells were split with accutase and plated on a Poly-L-Ornithine (PLO) (Sigma–Aldrich, P3655) dissolved in borate buffered saline (Sigma–Aldrich, 08059) coated plate in neuronal maturation media [BrainPhys (STEMCELL Technologies, 05790), 1× B27 supplement (Gibco, 17504044), 10 ng/ml Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (Peprotech, 450-02), 1 μg/ml laminin (R&D Systems, 3446-005-01), 10 ng/ml NT3 (Peprotech 450-03), and 2 μg/ml doxycycline].
L249: To plate neurons in Boyden chambers, six-well cell culture inserts with 1 μm pore size transparent PET membranes (Falcon, 353102) were coated with PLO overnight. After washing with water and fully drying chambers and holding six-well plates, the bottoms of the chambers were coated with 10 μg/ml laminin. After plating neurons in the final plate, half media changes were performed every other day. All neuron cultures were differentiated to day 17 post dox induction.
L250: Sphere differentiation: To differentiate iPSCs as neurospheres, iPSCs were plated in Corning 384 well round bottom ultra-low attachment spheroid microplates (Corning, 4516) after coating with anti-adherence rinsing solution (StemCell Technologies, 07010) and washing with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) twice. iPSCs were split with Accutase as normal and 10 000 cells were plated in neuronal induction media. The plate was centrifuged at 150 × g for 2 min to aggregate cells, then incubated at 37°C.
L251: On day 1, preheated neuronal induction medium was added. On day 3, recipient plates were coated with PLO and Laminin (15 μg/ml). A wide-orifice pipette was used to gently aspirate the neurosphere and place it in the recipient plate in neuronal maturation media.
L252: CRISPRi knockdown (KD): iPSCs were previously engineered to express dCas9 tagged to a KRAB transcriptional repressor domain under the CAG promoter [【48†30】]. Single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting TDP-43, or hnRNPA1, as well as a nontargeting (NT) guide were packaged into lentivirus for transduction of iPSCs as follows: PLO-coated plates were seeded with Lenti-X HEK cells in high glucose + GlutaMAX DMEM (Life Technologies, 10566024) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Sigma, TMS-013-B).
L253: The next day, arrayed transfection mixes were prepared as follows for 2.5 million cells on a six-well plate: 1.2 μg sgRNA plasmid and 2.4 μg packaging mix (1.6 μg psPAX2, 0.6 μg pMD2G, and 0.2 μg pAdVantage) were combined with 5 μl P3000 reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, L3000015) in 150 μl Opti-MEM (Gibco 31 985 070); 3.75 μl Lipofectamine 3000 Transfection Reagent (ThermoFisher, L3000075) was diluted into 150 μl Opti-MEM and incubated at room temperature for 5 min.
L254: DNA mixture was added to the diluted lipofectamine mixture and flicked to mix before incubating at room temperature for 30–45 min. Following incubation, mixture was added to cells in 1.5 ml DMEM + FBS dropwise with rocking to mix. The following day, media was changed to 3 ml fresh DMEM + FBS supplemented with 6 μl ViralBoost (Alstem VB100; diluted 1:500 in media).
L255: Two days later, media was transferred to a 15 ml conical tube, centrifuged for 5 min at 1100 × g, and supernatant was filtered with a 0.2 μm filter into a new tube to remove cell debris. Lenti-X Concentrator (Takara Bio, 631232) was added at 1:3, mixed, and incubated at 4°C for 2–4 days. After incubation, concentrated virus was pelleted by centrifugation at 1500 × g at 4°C for 45 min. Virus pellet was resuspended in cold PBS at 100 μl per ml of media (300 μl for 3 ml media).
L256: Virus was aliquoted and stored at −80°C until use. iPSCs were transduced with 100 μl virus per 100 000 cells at six-well scale (or 1 ml per 10 million cells at 15 cm plate scale) in E8 Chroman 1. Cells were checked for co-expressed fluorophore the following day and media was changed to fresh E8 Chroman 1. The following day, cells were treated with antibiotic (puromycin or blasticidin, depending on the resistance gene carried in the sgRNA plasmid) for 2 days.
L257: Subsequently, differentiation was initiated as usual. sgRNA sequences are as follows: non targeting control: GTCCACCCTTATCTAGGCTA, TARDBP: GGGAAGTCAGCCGTGAGACC, HNRNPA1: GAGAGAGGGCGAAGGTAGGC. For hnRNPA1-hnRNPA3 compensation immunofluorescence (IF), a dual guide plasmid was used [【49†31】].
L258: NT1 guide 1: GTCCCAGGCTCTCCACTATG, NT1 guide 2: GTACAGCTGGAAGGAAAGCC, NT2 guide 1: GGGACTCACGGTGTCATCGG, NT2 guide 2: GGGCTTCTGGCCGCTAGTAC, HNRNPA1 guide 1: GAGAGAGGGCGAAGGTAGGC, HNRNPA1 guide 2: GCGCGCAACAAAGGCTTGGG, HNRNPA3 guide 1: GTAATACCTCCTCCCCCCGG, HNRNPA3 guide 2: GCGGGCGAGGGGCCCCAAGG.
L259: ### RNA sequencing
L260: Neurite versus whole cell sequencing: Neurons grown in Boyden chambers were fractionated after washing in cold PBS by scraping the underside of chambers to collect neurites and the top of the chamber to collect the whole cell fraction. RNA was collected using the Qiagen RNeasy Miniprep kit (Qiagen, 74104).
L261: RNA was quantified with Qubit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 【50†Q32852†www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov】) and integrity evaluated by BioAnalyzer using the Pico kit (Agilent, 5067-1513); 10 ng of RNA per sample was used with the Takara Total RNA-seq Kit v2 – Pico Input Mammalian (634413) for wild-type (WT) samples and Takara Total RNA-seq Kit v3 – Pico Input Mammalian (634 485) for RBP KD samples and followed manufacturer instructions.
L262: Libraries were quantified by Qubit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 【51†Q32850†www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov】) and size confirmed with BioAnalyzer (Agilent, 5067-4626). Libraries were normalized to 3 nM, pooled, and iSeq performed to check normalization. When necessary, re-normalization was performed, and libraries were then sequenced (2 × 100 bp, depth about 50 M per sample) with Illumina NovaSeqS1 200.
L263: UPF1 KD and RNA sequencing: To knock down UPF1, sgRNAs targeting either a NT control guide (GTCCACCCTTATCTAGGCTA) or UPF1 (GGCCAGACGCAGACGCCCCC) were delivered to iPSC by lentiviral transduction as above. iNeurons were differentiated as above. On day 14 post doxycycline induction, iNeurons were collected and RNA was extracted with a RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen, 74104) following manufacturer’s instructions and including the on-column DNA digestion step.
L264: RNA concentrations were measured using Nanodrop and 500 ng of RNA was used for reverse transcription. Samples undergoing RNA sequencing were further assessed for RNA quality on a TapeStation 4200 (Agilent) and bands were quantified with TapeStation Systems Software v3.2 (Agilent). RNA integrity number for iNeurons was above 8.3.
L265: Sequencing libraries were prepared with polyA enrichment using a TruSeq Stranded mRNA Prep kit (Illumina, 20020594) and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 for NovaSeq 6000 machine at UCL Genomics at 2 × 150 bp, depth >40 M per sample.
L266: ### Proteomics
L267: Neurite versus whole cell proteomics: Boyden chambers were washed with cold PBS and neurites were scraped from the underside of the chamber. The top of the chamber was subsequently scraped as the whole cell fraction. Fractionated cells were pelleted, PBS removed, and cells flash frozen before proceeding to SP3/benzonase protocol as described [【52†32】].
L268: Briefly, samples were resuspended in SP3 buffer [50 mM Tris–HCI (pH = 8.0), 50 mM NaCl, 1% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), 1% Triton X-100, 1% NP-40, 1% Tween 20, 1% glycerol, 1% sodium deoxycholate (w/v), 5 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA; pH = 8.0, 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 5 KU benzonase, and 1 × complete protease inhibitor (Roche, 05892970001)], then shaken at 1200 rpm, 65°C for 30 min. Cell lysates were alkylated using 500 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) in the dark and then reduced by 500 mM DTT.
L269: Alkylated proteins were captured by hydrophilic magnetic beads using a KingFisher APEX robot, followed by a trypsin/LysC digestion in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate overnight at 37°C and 1200 rpm. Beads were removed using KingFisher APEX and digested peptides were lyophilized and reconstituted to 0.5 mg/ml with MS loading buffer (2% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid).
L270: The peptides were analyzed on an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer, coupled with FAIMS interface using data-independent acquisition (DIA) approach with scan range 400–1000 m/z, and 24 isolation windows (8 m/z per window).
L271: QuaNCAT: Neurons were starved of methionine (Met), lysine, and arginine amino acids in SILAC medium (Athena Enzyme Systems, 0423) for 45 min at 37°C. Four millimolar AHA was added to light and heavy media along with 0.5 mM lysine and 0.3 mM arginine with either the heavy or light isotope of both respectively. Neurons were incubated in the respective media (either light or heavy) for 2 h at 37°C before Met free media supplemented with 4 mM Met was added for 15 min.
L272: Following incubation, cells were placed on ice. Bead-based enrichment of AHA-containing proteins and subsequent on bead digestion were performed per manufacturer’s instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 【53†C10276†www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov】) with a few modifications. Briefly, urea lysis buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors (Roche, 05892970001) was added to each well lysis and shaken at 65°C at 1200 rpm for 30 min.
L273: The lysates were then centrifuged for 5 min and returned to ice while a 2× solution of 18 megaOhm water, component D (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 【54†C10416†www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov】) and Copper (II) sulfate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 【54†C10416†www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov】) were prepared. DCA was performed and 10% of lysate was collected as the input fraction and processed by SP3 as above.
L274: The remaining 90% of lysate was normalized, added to catalyst and beads solution, and rotated end over end at room temperature for 18 h. The following day, the reaction was centrifuged, and the supernatant was aspirated and collected for SP3 processing (flow through fraction). Water was added to the resin bead mixture and centrifuged again. SDS wash buffer and DTT were added to the beads and beads were vortexed briefly to resuspend the resin.
L275: The resin was heated at 70°C on a heating block for 15 min and then cooled to room temperature before being centrifuged for 5 min at 1000 × g, prior to aspirating the waste. IAA (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A39271) was added to each reaction, the reaction was then vortexed and incubated in the dark for 30 min. A 1 ml pipette was used to resuspend the resin solution and transfer to a gravity column.

Cells were incubated at 37°C overnight.
L311: Samples were washed twice with 2× SCC and then anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Biotium, 20015) at a 1:1000 dilution was added to the cells for 30 min at 37°C. Neurons were imaged with a 60× water immersion objective, 1.27 numerical aperture with a Nikon Ti2 spinning disc confocal, spinning disk at 4000 rpm for all colors.
L312: BFP was imaged with 300 ms exposure, excitation at 405 nm with laser power 70%, emission 455 nm. L474: ## Discussion
L475: mRNA transport and local translation enable neurons to respond rapidly to synaptic stimuli and are crucial for maintaining neuronal health. We found thousands of transcripts enriched in neurites, but fewer neurite-enriched proteins, which is similar to what others have seen in mouse iNeurons [【39†14】].

L377: ### Neurites have shorter isoforms that more often use proximal 3′ UTRs
L378: To determine whether transcripts transported to neurites have any common features that might contribute to their transport, we first used IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR, a tool that examines transcriptome-wide changes in certain types of alternative splicing [【69†47】], to evaluate the changes to isoforms in our WT neurons in neurites.
L379: When comparing the neurite to whole cell fractions, we found that genes identified in both compartments more often have NMD-sensitive transcripts in the neuritic fraction than the whole cell fraction (Fig. 【93†3A】). To investigate this further, we performed a GO analysis on the genes localized to neurites with NMD-sensitive transcripts. The NMD-sensitive transcripts are enriched for cytoplasmic, transport, and metabolism terms (Fig. 【93†3B】).
L380: Further, we analyzed genes that switch from transcripts that were predicted as NMD-sensitive in the neuritic fraction to NMD-insensitive in the whole cell fraction.
L381: In order to validate the predicted NMD sensitivity, we examined the expression of these isoforms in a UPF1 KD dataset, where lack of the crucial NMD factor UPF1 impairs the response, and confirmed that the ones predicted to be sensitive to NMD also significantly increase upon UPF1 KD, while predicted NMD-insensitive isoforms deriving from the same genes do not change (Fig. 【93†3C】).

L391: We observe an increased use of the most proximal UTR, the UTR closest to the end of the coding sequence, in the neurites compared to the whole cell (Fig. 【93†3D】 and E). Additionally, we analyzed transcripts enriched in the neuritic and whole cell fractions to identify potential RBPs regulating subcellular localization or post-transcriptional processes using Transite [【73†51】].
L392: This computational motif-based analysis tool infers RBPs driving global gene expression changes based on the RBP-binding motifs enriched in the 3′ UTRs of differentially expressed genes [【73†51】]. RBM8A was the highest scoring RBP that emerged from the Transite analysis of neurite-specific transcripts (Fig. 【93†3F】); SRSF7 had the highest enrichment score in the Transite analysis of whole cell-specific transcripts (Fig. 【93†3G】).
L393: These different RBP-binding motif enrichments in transcripts localized to neurites or whole cell and differential UTR use imply that these motifs and RBPs may be at least partially responsible for sorting transcripts to either remain in the whole cell or for transport to neurites.
L394: We further evaluated differences in 3′ UTRs of neurite localized transcripts. IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR finds that on average, neuritic transcripts are shorter or have shorter 3′ UTRs (Fig. 【93†3A】). REPAC, a tool to assess differential polyadenylation site usage between conditions [【74†52】], shows more transcripts with decreased length in neurites (Fig. 【93†3H】 and 【80†Supplementary Fig. S2F】 and G).
L395: APAlyzer, which examines 3′ APA, IPA, and gene expression [【75†53】], shows a larger number of transcripts with shorter 3′ UTRs and increased IPA in neurites (Fig. 【93†3H】 and I, and 【80†Supplementary Fig. S2H and I】). IPA may indicate more noncoding or truncated transcripts, which may be related to the increased NMD-sensitive transcripts we observe in neurites.
L396: APA-scan, a tool to identify 3′ UTR APA events [【76†54】], shows increased 3′ UTR truncations in neurites with a few potential 3′ UTR-APA events in whole cell (Fig. 【93†3H】 and 【80†Supplementary Fig. S2J】). Thus, in human i^{3}Neurons, neurite-localized transcripts tend to be shorter either as a whole transcript or have shorter 3′ UTRs.
L397: ### Newly synthesized proteins enriched for neurite localized transcripts
L398: To determine if the neurite localized transcripts are translated locally, we used two complementary mass spectrometry approaches quantifying the incorporation of heavy amino acids. The first, QuaNCAT [【95†62】], uses a Met analog with an azide group, L-azidohomoalanine (AHA), to enrich for newly synthesized proteins via click chemistry [【96†63】] onto an alkyne agarose bead (Fig. 【97†4A】). Neurons are pulsed with AHA and heavy arginine and lysine for 2 h prior to whole cell lysis (Fig. 【97†4A】).
L399: We used this short pulse to reduce the effect of protein degradation on heavy amino acid incorporation, ensuring all proteins that incorporate heavy amino acids were newly synthesized. As a control, we exposed cells to AHA without the presence of heavy amino acids (light samples). We also collected an input fraction prior to on-bead enrichment and a flow through fraction to determine the binding efficiency of the beads (Fig. 【97†4A】).
L400: There were few heavy proteins identified in the flow through and the QuaNCAT samples were enriched for heavy labeled peptides (【80†Supplementary Fig. S3A】). There are many fewer total proteins detected in the QuaNCAT group compared to the total proteins in the input or flowthrough, due to the enrichment of the small number that incorporate AHA and heavy amino acids (【80†Supplementary Fig. S3B】). We identified 267 heavy labeled proteins in the QuaNCAT samples (Fig. 【97†4B】).
L401: In comparison, we only identified 26 heavy labeled proteins in the input fraction and 34 in the flow through fraction (【80†Supplementary Fig. S3C–E】). As expected, many of the QuaNCAT enriched proteins are cytoskeletal proteins like ACTB and tubulins. We also identify several ribosomal proteins and RBPs like hnRNPA1, hnRNPK, and IGF2BP1. Indeed, pathway analysis of these proteins shows terms related to ALS and Parkinson’s disease (Fig. 【97†4C】), as was found for the neurite enriched transcripts (Fig.
L402: 【89†2B】), and the cellular component terms are highly related to cytoskeleton and axons/cell projections (Fig. 【97†4D】). As such, considering our short pulse time, it seems that the most frequently synthesized proteins in neurons are cytoskeletal proteins, RBPs like FUS, MATR3, NONO, TAF15, IGF2BP1, hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2B1, and hnRNPK.
L403: Interestingly, even though we performed this experiment on whole cells due to the amount of material needed for on-bead enrichment, many of the proteins we identified as newly synthesized are translated from transcripts that we found to be enriched neurites (Figs 【89†2】A and 【97†4B】).
L404: The enrichment of a transcript in neurites does not mean it could never be present in the soma and identification of these proteins as newly translated in whole cells does not necessarily mean that the translation occurred in neurites. However, this led us to hypothesize that at least some of this translation may be occurring in neurites.

L415: Given that almost a quarter of the newly synthesized proteins in whole cells are translated from transcripts enriched in neurites, we performed a pSILAC experiment on neurons grown in Boyden chambers to identify newly synthesized proteins in neurites. To identify newly synthesized proteins, both sides of the chambers were exposed to the same 2-h pulse of heavy arginine and lysine prior to neuron fractionation and trypsin digestion of proteins (Fig. 【97†4E】).
L416: As expected, due to the lack of enrichment and short pulse, fewer heavy labeled proteins were detected than light proteins (【80†Supplementary Fig. S3F】 and G). However, in comparing the heavy labeled proteins identified in the neurite and whole cell fractions, we were able to detect heavy labeled proteins significantly enriched in both fractions (【80†Supplementary Fig. S3H】).
L417: We find only 23 proteins enriched in the neurite fraction compared to the whole cell fraction; however, we can detect over 2000 heavy labeled proteins in the neurite fraction (Fig. 【97†4F】). This seeming disparity is expected as the whole cell fraction contains neurites as well as cell bodies, and while some of the highly translated proteins detected by QuaNCAT, like ACTB, are detected at high levels in neurites, their intensity is higher in the whole cell fraction.
L418: However, like QuaNCAT, many of the proteins encoded by neurite enriched transcripts are detected as containing heavy amino acids in the neurites (Figs 【89†2】A and 【97†4F】).
L419: While these newly synthesized proteins may have been transported from the cell body over the duration of the pulse, others have shown that most neurite enriched transcripts are translated locally [【39†14】], suggesting that the proteins we identify as both having neurite enriched transcripts and incorporating heavy amino acids in the neurites are indeed locally translated.
L420: Pathway analysis of neurite versus whole cell enriched proteins shows many nuclear and cell body related pathways and functions, reflective of the increased abundance of newly synthesized proteins in those compartments (【80†Supplementary Fig. S3I】 and J). However, pathway analysis of all proteins that were detected as newly synthesized in neurites shows pathways related to neuronal functions, including signaling pathways and axons, as well as pathways related to neurodegeneration (Fig. 【97†4G】).
L421: As such, many of the proteins encoded by transcripts enriched in neurites are translated locally. To confirm local translation in neurites, we used the SunTag translation assay [【101†64】, 【102†65】] to visualize translation of two proteins that were identified as incorporating heavy amino acids in neurites, RPS27A and SCG2. We were able to detect translation of each of these proteins in growth cones and neurites by SunTag (Fig.
L422: 【97†4】H and I), demonstrating that they, and possibly others, identified as incorporating heavy amino acids in neurites, are indeed locally translated.
L423: ### RBP KDs cause few protein mislocalizations but hnRNPA3 compensates for hnRNPA1 KD
L424: To understand the effect of loss-of-function of two FTD/ALS-associated RBPs on the neuritic proteome, we used CRISPRi [【48†30】] to knock down TDP-43 and hnRNPA1 by lentiviral sgRNA transduction of iPSCs prior to proceeding with neuron differentiation (Fig. 【103†5A】). Western blots and IF both confirm RBP KDs compared to a NT control guide (【80†Supplementary Fig. S4A–D】). We then fractionated RBP KD neurons and performed proteomics.
L425: Most of the variance between samples (49%–56%) can be explained by the neurite versus whole cell separation, rather than RBP KD (【80†Supplementary Fig. S4E】 and F). We observe decreased abundance of the knocked down RBP in both the neuritic and whole cell fractions (Fig. 【103†5B】–【103†E】), further confirming the efficacy of our KDs. TDP-43 KD leads to enrichment of more proteins in neurites (Fig.
L426: 【103†5B】), while hnRNPA1 KD leads to enrichment of more proteins in neurites compared to those that were depleted (Fig. 【103†5C】). For both TDP-43 and hnRNPA1 KD, we observe fewer protein changes in the whole cell fraction than the neurites, suggesting that loss of either of these proteins mostly affects the neuritic proteome (Fig. 【103†5】D and E). We did not observe many proteins that were inversely affected in each compartment (decrease in neurite and corresponding increase in whole cell, or vice versa).
L427: Pathway analysis identified terms related to the extracellular matrix in TDP-43 KD neurites and RNA processing in hnRNPA1 KD neurites (【80†Supplementary Fig. S4G】 and H). Surprisingly, for hnRNPA1 KD, we observed an increase in the related protein hnRNPA3 in both cellular compartments (Fig. 【103†5C】 and E). This increase suggests that hnRNPA3 may be compensating for the loss of expression of hnRNPA1.
L428: Indeed, KD of either hnRNPA1 or hnRNPA3 followed by IF shows an ∼50% increased protein level of the other protein (Fig. 【103†5F】–【103†H】). Of note, hnRNPA1 has a similar compensation mechanism with another family member, hnRNPA2 [【104†66】], suggesting these compensatory mechanisms may be prevalent among RBPs in the same family. Regardless, the compensation may explain the differences in effect size of hnRNPA1 KD than TDP-43 KD.

L439: ### RBP KD does not induce RNA mislocalization
L440: To determine the effect of RBP KD on mRNA localization in our iPSC-derived neurons, we performed RNA sequencing on fractionated NT and KD neurons. Overall, samples show similar expression efficiencies, but neurite samples tend to have higher fraction of reads aligning to rRNA (【80†Supplementary Fig. S5A】 and B). Samples had similar numbers of genes detected within an experiment (【80†Supplementary Fig. S5C】 and D).
L441: To confirm isolation of neurites from nuclei, we looked for the presence of snoRNAs in all samples. As expected, higher snoRNA amounts were observed in whole cell samples, but some snoRNAs and pre-mRNAs were detected in neurites, with more detected in the hnRNPA1 experiment compared to the TDP-43 experiment (【80†Supplementary Fig. S5E】 and F).
L442: Although some cross-contamination between compartments can occur in such experiments and may explain the presence of this category of these RNAs, snoRNAs are comparatively increased in the whole cell fractions, supporting the validity of this dataset analysis.
L443: Transcriptomics further validates our KDs, as both RBPs are significantly reduced in both the neuritic and whole cell fractions (Fig. 【107†6A】–【107†D】). Additionally, as expected for decreased TDP-43 levels [【108†67】, 【109†68】], STMN2 mRNA levels are significantly reduced in both fractions (Fig. 【107†6】A and C) [【110†69】]. Overall, TDP-43 KD shows the most genes with changes in abundance in both compartments (Fig. 【107†6】A and C).
L444: hnRNPA1 KD shows a more moderate effect on the neuritic and whole cell transcriptome, with some genes changing abundance in each compartment; interestingly, more genes are enriched than depleted (Fig. 【107†6】B and D). Of note, most of the difference in the samples (about 83% for each KD) comes from the cellular fraction, not the KD itself (【80†Supplementary Fig. S6A】 and B).

Title Altered mRNA transport and local translation in i3Neurons with RNA binding protein knockdown

Experiment type Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing
Summary Neurons rely on mRNA transport and local translation to facilitate rapid protein synthesis in processes far from the cell body. These processes allow precise spatial and temporal control of translation and are mediated by RNA binding proteins (RBPs), including those associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Here, we use proteomics, transcriptomics, and microscopy to investigate the impact of RBP depletion on mRNA transport and local translation in iPSC-derived neurons. We find thousands of transcripts enriched in neurites and that many of these transcripts are locally translated, possibly due to the shorter length of transcripts in neurites. Loss of frontotemporal dementia/amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (FTD/ALS)-associated RBPs TDP-43 and hnRNPA1 lead to distinct alterations in the neuritic proteome and transcriptome. TDP-43 knockdown (KD) leads to slightly increased neuritic mRNA and translation. In contrast, hnRNPA1 leads to more moderate effects on local mRNA profiles, possibly due to compensation by hnRNPA3. These results highlight the crucial role of FTD/ALS-associated RBPs in mRNA transport and local translation in neurons and the importance of these processes in neuron health and disease.
 
Overall design i3Neurons grown in Boyden chambers were split into soma- and neurite-fractions and had their transcriptomes assessed via RNA-seq. We include samples with no further treatment (no-treatment), as well as CRISPRi knockdown of hnRNPA1 or TDP-43, in addition to non-targeting sgRNA controls.
